speaker: Speaker 1
words: 22nd of March, 1975. This is Isabelle Miller. I'm interviewing Hollis Edgerton on the 22nd of March, 1975. All right, so Hollis, you're a student in Lewis and Clark

speaker: Speaker 2
words: College, right?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What year is that?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: 22nd.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: So you're second year in general education. OK, what are some of the advantages and disadvantages you see of living in a rural area?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, I really don't see, well, sometimes I complain about living on the farm. But like my mom said, in her mind, she knew she was going to live on the farm. And I think I'm going to live on the farm, too. Because I think kids should be based on the farm.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Or where there's an open space. And you have a chance to be alone when you want to be.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: You can just go out and think by yourself.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And you, of course, don't feel isolated now, like your grandmother did, of course. You have your own car.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I do pretty much what I want.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: You go to school in Lewiston, which is about 30 miles away?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah, about 30. But I still like to get my parents' approval. Like two weekends ago, I went down to Idaho Falls. So I called Mom and asked if it was all right up there.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And she goes, yeah.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: You think you can afford it?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: You get to manage your own money?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, I work. Well, during the summer, I worked for Dad. Last year, I worked up in the bakery in Rose

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Hours for a few weeks.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Then I worked for this lady for about a month. So in Idaho.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: So you earned your own money. What did you do in Rose Hours Bakery?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I sold food and just been a clerk. Cleaned up. Really exciting.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Have you held any other jobs? No.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: That's my first away.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: You lived in Moscow then? Or did you go back and forth?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, I drove back and forth.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh, drove back and forth in your own car. Did your parents buy this car for you when you graduated?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, it was theirs. Until they got the new one. Then they gave me the old one.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: So you kind of inherited it then? Yeah.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: It's an old 65 Mercury that still runs beautifully. And of course, you couldn't get anything on it. It's a tribute. So it's yours too. And it gets me where I want to go sometimes.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Do you live in a residence hall?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yes, I do. There's only one girls hall down there in my residence.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Do you plan to work in the summertime?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah, I guess so. I have a chance of working down there, helping clean the buildings down on campus. So I think I might do that.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: If you don't do that, you'll come home and help your mother camp?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, yeah. Yeah, help my dad. I drive truck down here.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Is that what you like to do best?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Not really. But since I'm the only girl, I get stuck driving truck.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Because you can't lift hay bales.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, I can lift hay bales. But I go too slow. My brother's yelling at me. So of course, I yell right back at him.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: How have you felt about the chores

speaker: Speaker 2
words: that you've done with your brothers

speaker: Speaker 1
words: as you were growing up? Is there any real differences in the kind of work you do?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, I don't think so. Yeah, you never have to do chores outside in the winter to help me, really. Well, yeah. And then when Nick had those rabbits, oh, I had them. He never fed them.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I always fed them.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: They usually do all the chores.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: How do you feel about being a girl?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: All right, I guess.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Have you ever wished you were a boy?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Sometimes I wish I were. Sometimes I'm glad I'm a girl.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What were some of the reasons you wished you were a boy?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Didn't have to clean house.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Didn't have to clean barns.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah, so that's good. The advantage of being a girl, you don't have to clean barns.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I don't have to clean barns. What are the times you really feel good? Can you think of any time when you feel really good about being a girl?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, I get more like mom's in the mood. She makes me new clothes. And she never makes boys any clothes, so that's it for me.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: It's a little more fun to sew girls' clothes than boys' clothes. It's more fun to sew. If you got married and had children, would you more or less want to raise them the way you can raise them? Yeah. You said you thought, pretty sure you'd raise them in a farm.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah, I probably would. Living down in Wilson all week just like this to you. You didn't come home from the farm. You really appreciate the farm.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Certainly, the clear air.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, yeah.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And being able to look out and see a nice view. You can't do that in town. Yeah. What do you, you're studying most of the time down there?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I put you on the spot. I wondered if you were honest about that.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Half. Well, half and half. Now I'm studying a little bit more, because it's getting close to the end of school. I go out once in a while with the girls, you know, have some beers. We'll have fun.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Do you have a definite goal in mind? You're just preparing to do some kind of work before you marry, or what?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I really don't know what I want.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Do you really plan to get married?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I want to get married someday, but not too soon. I want to wait till I'm ready. I really don't know what I want to do.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: But you feel obligated to prepare to do something, at least that you can make a living. Yeah. At least you know you're going to be pushed out of home

speaker: Speaker 2
words: sometime.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I expect that you'll do something. So you do things with girls down there, like have a beer or something. Any other movies?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Do you go to movies? Oh, we go to movies once in a while.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And you go to ball games when you're home.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, yeah. I went to most of the ball games down there, home ball games. Because I really like basketball. It's the only sport I really like.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: You play it, or you watch it?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, if I had a chance, I would play it. But down there, they really don't.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: They don't have a very well-developed program?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Not really. But I love to watch it.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Do they have more opportunities for men in athletics?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah, I guess. It's the only sports they have down in the state for basketball.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: They don't have a girls team, so.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Not really.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And they didn't have an exposed gender series?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: They came through high school.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Not too much, no.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Do you think this is something that could be changed? That you would, like some others on the school board, and kind of looking toward maybe developing that area? Do you think more girls would participate at that opportunity?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, I don't know. I really can't say. Like in high school, I wanted to play basketball. And the coach, the girls coach, didn't like me, I guess. So I just didn't put her on the team. But I think if they had a chance, they would.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I think. Do you think there's a feeling among girls that they can't do anything physical at a high, you know, develop their physical ability?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, I really don't know.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I guess sometimes I've observed girls standing around the schoolyard and talking, whereas boys are out running and doing things. What do you think makes that difference?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I guess I really don't know. I guess girls like to talk. I don't know. Girls are known to do that. Guys think, oh, girls like to talk.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: But they certainly see some benefits that people get from physical activity. You might think the girls get the same benefit if they had the opportunity.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I think they'll get to be more and more of the girls sports.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: If they have more opportunities where they'll find out how much fun it is. Well, that was just something that I haven't talked to a girl your age for a while. And I wonder how you felt about that. You talked a little bit about what you do around home. You help Ken, you help in the garden, you do housework, and drive trucks, and when the opportunity is necessary. So you feel as though you can do just about anything with boys.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I think I can.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: But since you have four brothers, you just really haven't taken care of that part of it. And you've talked a little bit about preparing to have a job and that you'll work some. Do you see it as necessary, even though you get married, that you're able to do? Have you thought about the possibility that your husband not always being able to support you?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Not really. I really haven't thought about it. You're not even marrying a rich man, so she doesn't know. Like all girls do. Yeah.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Lots of luck.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Lots of my sister-in-law said. You'll find him. I know.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What would be your ideal job? What would be my ideal job? If you could have, right now, could imagine that whatever you decide to do, you'd be successful in it, and you'd have your choice of going anywhere, anything. What would be the most ideal job you could have?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, in high school, I always wanted to be a teacher, an elementary teacher. I was first grade, or even a kindergarten teacher, because I love little kids. And maybe a teacher. But now, I don't think I want to be a teacher. I don't know.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What's kind of changed your mind?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, the classes I have to take.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Education classes aren't the most important thing.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I have to take speech, and I'm not good at getting to turn people and talk.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Do you have anybody down there that talks to you about your vocational plans? Do you have counselors down there?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I have an advisor. But he doesn't talk to me about that very much.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Mostly it's decisions on what to take, maybe. Yeah. There's no women's counselor down there?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, yeah. We have a woman counselor. Well, yeah. But nobody ever goes to see her, I guess. I don't know why. How about Lorraine? Does she ever talk to you about? No. Whenever she's there. She's their house mother, I guess you could say. Yeah.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Uh-huh. In the residence hall. Yeah. So you really don't know, have you ever taken any vocational tests or interest tests or anything?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, no, I think I have. I took a lot of tests in high school. You sure you didn't high school, huh? You never did do those. But I don't know.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: You took probably some achievement tests in high school.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah, I took a lot of those in high school.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did you get the results on that back? Talked to somebody about?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, not yet.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: So you don't really know what your strong subjects are and what your weak ones are?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, I know what my weak one is. Math. I can not do math. It's a bother. Uh-huh.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Uh-huh. I don't know.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Math just blows my mind. Yeah.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did they ever say what help you can get from your counselor

speaker: Speaker 2
words: if you'd go to them? No.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I'm starting to think the name of the woman. Debbie, somebody.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Daryl Wilson? Tammy Bishop.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Tammy Bishop, that's the name. What did they advertise? What kind of services did she offer? Is she just there?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: She's just there if you want to go talk to her. You have any problems and you can't talk over with your house or with anybody else?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: But they don't say what kind of problems, just in general.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Just general problems.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Well, this is, you know, aside from this, but you might go and ask about some interactive tasks, a tutor or some of them. And that might give you some idea of what the things, by identifying things you'd like to do in recreation in your daily life, you can identify certain work areas that might be more interesting to you than others. You might follow up on that. Anyway, it might be interesting to go see what she has to offer you, too. Because it doesn't sound like your advisor's giving you too much help.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, he just, you know, asks me what classes I want to take and so on.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Well, he's so busy.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah, he's never around. He's a teacher. And he takes classes himself.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: So he's really not available very much, only when you're preparing your program for the next semester, I suppose.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: That's a problem.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: You know, I should think that you might just find that Kenny Bishop could be helpful. At least she's there more and fully available to you. And they should have some interesting tasks, which I think it'd be fun to take for your own interest. I know. Do you read any different magazines and newspapers in your family? No.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I read about the same. Well, I read the newspaper once in a while. The magazine, newspaper, it's interesting. But I really don't read that much, that many books.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Other than for classes.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I start learning all these books.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: If you don't come home for a weekend, what do you do? Starve. That's telling me why you come home.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: There's really nothing you can do down there.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: There are some girls who stay the whole weekend.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, yeah. They live so far away. Yeah.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Do they study or? Yeah.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Most of them do.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: So they could get caught up on everything then. It's pretty quiet.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Usually it's the nursing students that study. That dorm, it's filled mostly with nursing students. It's really nice. And then there's times when I'm like, well, get away from all the girls. Let's eat a decent meal. Uh-huh. That's what you've done there too.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Institutional food doesn't. And the cooking, the quantities.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: It doesn't stick with you.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Not as a same type thing your mother cooks at home. You get enough to eat?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Do you have plenty? Oh, yeah. You get enough. But like half an hour later, you're starving. Up here, I can eat, eat, and fold.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And for a few hours, then you start eating. Yeah.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I love to eat, so.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Do you have a regular gym program down there now? Or do you have to participate in fiscal ed at all?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: You don't have to. Well, the first, you have to take PE the first year. And I think you take four semesters, three semesters, PE. That's my plan.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Uh-huh. You said you were thinking about switching over into the voc ed.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Voc ed.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Voc ed. Yeah. Oh, what area would you?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, just like typing or like that.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: So develop really a job-oriented skill. That's where you are right now. Don't really see the way to go into teaching, or you've kind of changed your mind about that. I think, too, in your, Tammy Bishop ought to have some books on other occupations. Occupational Outlook Handbook, for instance. Do you know that she has something?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I don't know if she does or not. She might.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: It might be fun just to go in there and leaf through some of the materials they have to see what others.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: She comes up to the dorm once in a while and has like a grime session.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Mm-hmm.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: So that's the only time we ever see her. Uh-huh. And then she'd go to her office.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And she usually ends up, I think, come over to my office and see what we have. Mm-hmm. But you've never done that yet?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, not yet. Uh-huh.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did you watch TV down there?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Um, not as much as I used to. I don't know. I used to. Like I said before, I used to go out. But sometimes I do, yeah. Uh-huh.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Do you have favorite programs?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Um, I mean, during the day or during the night?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Any time. Any time you want.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, there's two soap operas we've watched down there. Two main ones all the girls like to watch. Then at nighttime, I like Madge. You know, the comedy kind of show.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Situational comedy.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah, and emergency, you know, like that.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Do a lot of the girls in the residence hall watch TV with you? Yeah. So it's a kind of recreational thing. Yeah. Mm-hmm. How many women live in the hall?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: About 56.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: This is the one residence hall? Do some live out in apartments in town? Yeah. Do they, this is the only place that girl students live? Or do they have the option of living out in the town? I think there's a lot of them in apartments.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Or with their own families.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah, there's a lot of local girls down there that live at home. Uh-huh. Thank you.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: You plan to marry eventually, but you haven't really made too many plans. You haven't met anybody that you'd be interested in?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No. Not really.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What do you think's important in having a husband? What would be your ideal husband?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Rose Redford. Oh. Well. He has to be taller than me. That's the main thing I'm looking for.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Do you feel like you're unusually tall?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh. You feel like you know that.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: How tall are you?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: About 5'15". And, yeah, I don't know. But I'm usually, I'm looking for a guy taller than about 6'0". You know, like my brother. They're all taller than you.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Just the younger ones.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, he's getting up there. So, um, he has to be kind, of course. Kind of. Kind of like my dad. You know, he can, um, I don't know what I want to say. Um, they're not putting him down. Not really. No. Um, who can support the family like my dad does.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Uh-huh. Yeah. You wouldn't, you would not expect to support, help support the family.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, if I had to, I...

speaker: Speaker 1
words: But ideally, you wouldn't really want to.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, not really.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: You'd rather, uh, do like your mother did, get married and stay at home and raise children. That's the way you see it. So, if you had a job, it would be until you got married, or it would be kind of back up if you had to do anything. That's the way you see it. How about decisions in making family life? Would you like to have equal say in everything? Yeah. That's important to you. You wouldn't want to have a man that would decide everything and let you know. No.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I mean, I think women have the right to say what they feel. Uh-huh.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And if they don't like what's going on, they should be, they should...

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Tell them. If they don't like it.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Uh-huh. And be able to make some changes in that way. If the husband doesn't agree with it, well,

speaker: Speaker 2
words: then I guess you just drop the subject until you can agree on it. Well, pick a subject you both agree on.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: How about talking about it, maybe looking at all sides. Yeah. That might be a possible way to work it out. Uh-huh. Well, how do you feel looking at, say, you must know something about your grandmother's life, and your mother's life, and now as you project ahead, who has the most opportunities, you?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Um, I really don't know much about my grandmother's life. And my mom's life? Oh, I don't know how to put it. Um, ooh, that's tough. Um, I really don't know. I think... I don't know what to say about that.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: If you got married and had five children and were living like your mother is now, do you think that would be a good life?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, yeah. I think it would. I think I have about the same opportunities as my mom, maybe a little bit more, I don't know. I don't know.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: So it's up to you what you want to make out of your life. Yeah, I do. You feel that pretty much now? Yeah. You just get some ideas and a direction. Yeah. Is there anything else you'd like to tell about the way things appear to you right now?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, I don't think there's anything.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Do you ever think much about the women's movement, the liberation, anything?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: You don't care too much about that, do you?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, I really don't care about it.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: The students aren't much into that.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Not down there.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Is there a dramatics teacher down at Shirley? Hannigan.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Hannigan. Hannigan. I think that's her name.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Do you have her for speech? No. She's kind of, I think, involved in this. Do you ever hear very much from her? Are there some students involved in this?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: There's some, I guess. I don't think. Nobody at the dorm, I don't think. If you hear about her being a liberated woman and things.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What does that mean to you?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I haven't. I'm being free, I guess. I don't know.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: You don't feel unfree yourself. No. That doesn't really mean anything to you. I guess this kind of gets into something I'd kind of like to ask. When we came down here and gave the presentation in Genesis, we heard that some people did not want their girls to come to us because it was such a women radical. Had you heard anything like that? Lily had some feedback on that. And I wondered if that's a general opinion of some people in Genesis. Oh, I don't know. I would guess. I wouldn't think so from the women, anyway. Possibly from the men. In Moscow, we hear some of the old-time farmers in Genesis are pretty conservative. I guess some of the German background might contribute to that. Is that? I'm certain there wasn't anything in the presentation, was there, that invited them? No, I wouldn't think so at all. But we just heard a few things here and there that was, that at least they were expecting some radical stuff from the university. Oh, were they? Yes, I think Genesis has a chip on the shoulder as far as the university is concerned. I know I certainly do. And so that might have been part of it. But I think that the majority of women in Genesis are, well, now of course each person sees things as they want to. But I think that the majority of women are very happy. They feel pretty free, they manage their lives. Is that the way it looks to me, anyway? Just saying, well, women around, they seem to be able to pretty much do what they want to do. And they all seem to be pretty satisfied with their lot in life. That they have to be home, say, by 6 o'clock to fix dinner. But my gosh, that's not so difficult. It's not very restrictive. No. But I suppose if I was an unhappy woman, then I would associate with other women who were, and I might have a very different thought of. What do you mean by having a chip on your shoulder about the university? Oh, I think that it's happened a couple of times that they've, well, I don't know how to say it, but we don't like for them to interfere too much with the school. Oh. I think.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: And some of the,

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I think they're very happy in science. Yeah.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: And the people at Genesis, well, you'll find this in any small town. I don't mean just Genesis, any small town. They think they're doing pretty good the way things are.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: They know what their needs are better than someone from outside.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: And I do know that they don't really care to get first-year teachers out of the university because they are teaching up here now in education too much of this. For even in the classroom, when you get 30 little kids.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did you make the decision to go to Lewis & Clark rather than the university?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: It's a smaller school.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And that appears to be more important.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Because at the university I felt like I started getting lost. And their classes are harder and L.C.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Where would you, you didn't get the results on your achievement test, but where do you think you stood in relation to other people in your class?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I don't know. Maybe in the middle.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: About the middle.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: And then lower. Okay.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: So you felt like you probably couldn't do the best at the university that probably you'd be able to do better at Lewis & Clark for what you wanted. But if you decide on a goal now that could be met only at the university, would you see that as an option to go there?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I don't know. It depends. Well, it depends if I have the money to go to the university. Is that something?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Is it a lot more expensive than Lewis & Clark?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I think it is.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Uh-huh. Is it?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I don't know if it's convenient to get a tuition. Well, maybe not. I don't know. But I think it is.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What does it cost to go to Lewis & Clark?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, it's just... No. It seems like your tuition is $125. $125.

speaker: Speaker 1
